rv.q: And yet, somehow, Stoppard, Russell Beale and Tennyson find a light in Housman you might never have imagined.
The quicksilver Russell Beale is a vocal glory, leaping in a breath from flute to poignant bassoon, from wit to sorrow.
McIntyre funnels a stream of fine performances, with many actors multi-roling, into a play that, for the most part, sweeps the audience away.
He wears his learning on his sleeve but beneath that beats a heart and electrifying artistic purpose.
This first London revival of that much-admired 1997 play offers plenty of pleasures, not least a characteristically lucid and tender central turn from Simon Russell Beale.

Matthew Tennyson gives us a heated young Housman, while Beale portrays everything from suppressed desolation to waspish put-downs with his customary deftness. At almost three hours, the play is a little wearing, but there are always Stoppard’s great jokes.
It’s in this tone that the play continues, keeping an otherwise potentially alienated audience enthralled by its carefully timed, easy wit.
